title: Mandache's question on the optimal exponent for m(δ)
statement_text: What is the optimal exponent $\alpha$ such that $m(\delta) \sim \delta^\alpha$ as $\delta \to 0$, where $m(\delta)$ denotes the minimum triforce density $\int_{[0,1]^6} W(x',y,z)W(x,y',z)W(x,y,z')\,dx\,dy\,dz\,dx'\,dy'\,dz'$ among all measurable $W:[0,1]^3\to[0,1]$ with $\int W = \delta$?
context_text: Mandache showed that $\delta^4 \leq m(\delta) \lesssim \delta^{3.13}$ and asked what the optimal exponent on $\delta$ is. This question motivates the paper's main results on triforce densities.
paper_contribution: Proves that the optimal exponent is $4$: $m(\delta) = \delta^{4-o(1)}$ and $m(\delta) = \omega(\delta^4)$ as $\delta \to 0$ (Theorem 1.2), settling Mandache's question.

title: Green's Problem 19 (Popular Corners)
statement_text: Determine $M(\delta)$, the maximum constant such that for every $\varepsilon > 0$ and every sufficiently large $n$, every $A \subseteq G \times G$ with $|A| \geq \delta|G|^2$ contains at least $(M(\delta) - \varepsilon)|G|^2$ corners $(x,y),(x+d,y),(x,y+d) \in A$ for some nonzero $d \in G$.
context_text: Ben Green posed this problem in his collection of open problems. Mandache and Chu had established that the naive extension (finding as many corners as in the random case) fails, but the correct order of $M(\delta)$ was open.
paper_contribution: Corollary 1.3 proves $M(\delta) \leq \delta^{4-o(1)}$ for all sequences of finite abelian groups $G_n$ with $|G_n| \to \infty$, and $M(\delta) = \omega(\delta^4)$ for $G_n = \mathbb{F}_p^n$ with fixed prime $p$, thereby solving the problem.
notes: PDF source — math may be garbled. The paper states 'This result solves Problem 19 from Ben Green's collection of open problems [11]'; the exact verbatim statement of Problem 19 is not reproduced in the paper, so the statement above is reconstructed from context.

title: Informal question on Behrend-style sets avoiding affine patterns with mixed-sign coefficients
statement_text: We do not know if there are subsets of $[N]$, in the style of Behrend's construction, with $N^{1-o(1)}$ elements avoiding such patterns, i.e. avoiding (non-trivial) solutions of a linear equation $a_1x_1+a_2x_2+a_3x_3+a_4x_4=0$ with $a_1+a_2+a_3+a_4=0$ and two positive and two negative coefficients (e.g., $2x + 2y = 3w + z$).
context_text: $[N]=\{1,\dots,N\}$. Behrend's construction gives subsets of $[N]$ of size $N^{1-o(1)}$ (density $e^{-O(\sqrt{\log N})}$) with no 3-term arithmetic progression, i.e. no non-trivial solution of $x+z=2y$. A popular difference for a pattern in a set $A$ is a common difference $d\ne0$ shared by many copies of the pattern in $A$ (about as many as in a random set of the same density). Bergelson, Host, Kra and Ruzsa constructed sets without popular differences for $k$-term progressions, $k\ge5$, from Behrend-type sets, while Green and Tao's positive result for 4-term progressions relies on the identity $P(0)-3P(1)+3P(2)-P(3)=0$ for quadratic $P$, which has a symmetric form $P(0)-3P(1)=P(3)-3P(2)$. The authors construct sets $A\subseteq[N]^3$ of density $\delta$ in which every $d\ne0$ is the common difference of at most $\delta^{c\log(1/\delta)}N^3$ three-dimensional corners $(x,y,z),(x+d,y,z),(x,y+d,z),(x,y,z+d)$. They explain that a 3-dimensional corner projects to other 4-term patterns such as $x,x+y,x+2y,x+4y$, and that the Bergelson–Host–Kra–Ruzsa approach would need an identity expressing one value $P(b_i)$ as a convex combination of the others for all quadratic $P$; but any identity $a_1P(b_1)+\dots+a_4P(b_4)=0$ valid for all quadratic $P$, with $a_1+\dots+a_4=0$, distinct $b_i$ and not all $a_i$ zero, must have two positive and two negative $a_i$ (by Lagrange interpolation). The paper does not spell out what 'avoiding' means for such a pattern; presumably no non-trivial solution of the corresponding linear equation. This is additive combinatorics rather than graph theory.

title: Informal conjecture on extending Mandache's Theorem 1.1 to all abelian groups
statement_text: It seems likely that Mandache's lower bound $M(\delta) \geq m_{\mathrm{convex}}(\delta)$, proved for $G_n=\mathbb{F}_p^n$ with fixed prime $p$, can be extended to all sequences of finite abelian groups via Bohr sets, though as far as we know this has not yet been worked out.
context_text: A corner in $G\times G$, for an abelian group $G$, is a triple $(x,y),(x+d,y),(x,y+d)$ with $d\ne0$; for $A\subseteq G\times G$, $S_d(A)=\{(x,y):(x,y),(x+d,y),(x,y+d)\in A\}$, so $|S_d(A)|$ counts corners of common difference $d$. For a sequence of finite abelian groups $G=G_n$ with $|G_n|\to\infty$, $M(\delta)$ is the largest number such that for every $\epsilon>0$ and $n$ large, every $A\subseteq G\times G$ with $|A|\ge\delta|G|^2$ has some $d\ne0$ with $|S_d(A)|\ge(M(\delta)-\epsilon)|G|^2$ (a popular difference). The triforce is the 3-uniform hypergraph on 6 vertices with edges $\{1,2,3'\},\{1,2',3\},\{1',2,3\}$; for measurable $W:[0,1]^3\to[0,1]$ its density is $\int W(x',y,z)W(x,y',z)W(x,y,z')\,dx\,dy\,dz\,dx'\,dy'\,dz'$, and $m(\delta)$ is the minimum triforce density over all $W$ with $\int W=\delta$. Mandache proved $M(\delta)\le m(\delta)$ for all $G_n$ (by a random construction), and that for $G_n=\mathbb{F}_p^n$ with $p$ a fixed prime, $M(\delta)\ge m_{\mathrm{convex}}(\delta)$ for every convex function $m_{\mathrm{convex}}\le m$ pointwise, via an arithmetic regularity argument combined with Fourier-analytic ideas. The authors prove $m(\delta)=\delta^{4-o(1)}$ and $m(\delta)=\omega(\delta^4)$, hence $M(\delta)\le\delta^{4-o(1)}$ for all $G_n$ and $M(\delta)=\omega(\delta^4)$ for $\mathbb{F}_p^n$; the expected extension would give the lower bound for all abelian groups. They also show that popular differences fail for 3-dimensional corners. This is additive combinatorics rather than graph theory.
